description: Standard fitness tests, their protocols, and how to compare results against normative data.
content_html:
Why Fitness Testing Matters

Fitness testing gives coaches and athletes a precise picture of current physical condition. Without measurement, training decisions rely on guesswork. With structured testing, a coach can identify which components of fitness are strengths and which need attention, establish a baseline from which improvement is tracked, compare results against national norms, and motivate athletes with concrete targets. There are several reasons to carry out fitness tests: to identify strengths and weaknesses, to monitor improvement over time, to establish a starting level of fitness, to inform training requirements, to compare results against norms or previous personal bests, and to motivate athletes and help them set realistic goals.

Key Fact

Six reasons for fitness testing: (1) identify strengths and weaknesses, (2) monitor improvement, (3) establish a baseline, (4) inform training needs, (5) compare to norms, (6) motivate and set realistic goals. In the exam, giving just one reason earns only part marks — learn the full list.

Cardiovascular Endurance Tests

Three tests assess cardiovascular endurance. The Cooper 12-minute run test requires the participant to run as far as possible in 12 minutes on a flat, measured course. The distance covered is recorded and compared against age and gender normative tables. The Cooper 12-minute swim test follows the same principle in the water. The Harvard Step Test requires the participant to step up and down on a 30 cm bench for 5 minutes at a set pace. One minute after stopping, the heart rate is measured. A lower heart rate indicates a more efficient cardiovascular system. The fitness index is calculated and compared against normative data.

Agility, Strength, Muscular Endurance and Flexibility Tests

The Illinois agility run test measures agility. The participant starts lying face down and, on the signal, sprints up and back along a course of cones placed 5 metres apart, weaving between cones in the middle section. The time taken is recorded and compared against normative data. Shorter times indicate greater agility.

Grip strength is measured using a grip dynamometer. The participant squeezes the device as hard as possible; the result is recorded in kilograms and compared to normative tables.

Muscular endurance is assessed using one-minute tests. In the one-minute sit-up test, the participant performs as many full sit-ups as possible in 60 seconds with a partner holding their feet. In the one-minute press-up test, the participant performs as many full press-ups as possible in 60 seconds, maintaining correct form throughout. Higher numbers indicate greater muscular endurance.

Flexibility is measured using the sit and reach test. The participant sits with their legs straight against a measuring box, feet flat against the base, and reaches forward along the measuring scale as far as possible. The furthest point reached (in centimetres) is recorded. A greater score indicates greater lower back and hamstring flexibility.

Speed and Power Tests

The 30-metre sprint test measures speed. The participant sprints 30 metres from a standing start; the time is recorded using either a stopwatch or electronic timing gates. A lower time indicates greater speed. The vertical jump test measures power. The participant stands next to a wall, reaches up to mark their standing reach, then jumps as high as possible and touches the wall at the peak of the jump. The difference between the two marks, in centimetres, represents the jump height. A higher jump indicates greater leg power.

Key Fact

Test-to-component pairings: Cooper 12-minute run/swim → cardiovascular endurance; Harvard Step Test → cardiovascular endurance; Illinois agility run → agility; grip dynamometer → strength; one-minute sit-up/press-up → muscular endurance; 30 m sprint → speed; vertical jump → power; sit and reach → flexibility.

Normative data tables provide pre-established ranges of results for different age groups and genders. For example, a Cooper 12-minute run normative table might indicate that a 16-year-old male who covers 2,400 metres or more scores in the “excellent” category, while 1,800–2,000 metres is “below average.” Comparing an individual’s result to normative data tells the coach whether the performer is stronger or weaker than the population average in that component. It is important to use the correct normative table — age and gender must match, because expected results vary significantly between groups. Data interpretation questions in the exam will often ask you to compare a result to a provided table and draw a conclusion about the performer’s fitness level.

A common data task is calculating the percentage improvement between two test results. The formula is:

Percentage improvement = ((new score − original score) ÷ original score) × 100

Example: a student’s vertical jump improves from 40 cm to 47 cm after a 6-week plyometric programme. Percentage improvement = ((47 − 40) ÷ 40) × 100 = (7 ÷ 40) × 100 = 17.5%. Always show units in your final answer (in this case, %). Calculators are permitted in the written examination, but you still need to show your working clearly.
exam_tip_html: For data interpretation questions, follow the three-step rule that examiners reward: (1) quote a specific figure with units from the data, (2) make a comparison or identify a trend (e.g. compare to normative data or a previous result), (3) state the sporting or training implication. Simply writing “the score increased” without a number, or writing a number without a comparison, each lose a mark. For calculation questions involving percentage improvement, always show the formula, then the substitution, then the final answer with a percentage sign. On questions asking you to select the most appropriate fitness test for a sport, you must justify your choice by linking the test to the relevant component of fitness required in that sport.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Fitness tests serve six purposes: identifying strengths/weaknesses, monitoring progress, establishing baselines, informing training, comparing to norms, and motivating athletes.
  • Each fitness test is matched to one specific component: Cooper run/swim and Harvard Step Test measure cardiovascular endurance; Illinois agility run measures agility; grip dynamometer measures strength; one-minute sit-up/press-up measure muscular endurance; 30 m sprint measures speed; vertical jump measures power; sit and reach measures flexibility.
  • Normative data allows an individual’s result to be compared against population averages; percentage improvement is calculated as (new − old) ÷ old × 100.

practice_questions.text:
Which fitness test is used to measure agility?
A) Harvard Step Test
B) Vertical jump test
C) Illinois agility run test
D) Sit and reach test
practice_questions.marks: C) Illinois agility run test [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two reasons why a coach might use fitness testing with a group of athletes.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: to identify strengths and weaknesses; to monitor improvement over time; to establish a starting level of fitness; to inform training needs; to compare results against normative data; to motivate athletes and help set realistic goals.

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old club-level swimmer achieves a score of 34 cm in the sit and reach test. The normative data table shows that 36-40 cm is 'above average' for this age group. Calculate the percentage improvement needed to reach the lower boundary of 'above average'.
practice_questions.marks: Formula applied: ((36 - 34) / 34) x 100 (1 mark for correct working); = 5.88% (accept 5.9% or 6%), with percentage sign (1 mark for correct answer with units).

practice_questions.text: Describe the protocol for the Cooper 12-minute run test and explain how the results are interpreted.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: participant runs as far as possible in 12 minutes on a flat, measured course (1); the distance covered in metres is recorded at the end of 12 minutes (1); the result is compared against age- and gender-matched normative data tables to determine the fitness category (e.g. excellent, above average, average, below average, poor) (1).

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows the sit-up test results of four students before and after an 8-week training programme.

Student | Before (sit-ups/min) | After (sit-ups/min)
Aisha   | 25                  | 31
Dylan   | 18                  | 22
Fatima  | 30                  | 35
Jordan  | 22                  | 28

Interpret the data to identify which student showed the greatest percentage improvement in muscular endurance.
practice_questions.marks:
Calculate percentage improvement for each student:
Aisha: (31-25)/25 x 100 = 24% (1)
Dylan: (22-18)/18 x 100 = 22.2% (1)
Fatima: (35-30)/30 x 100 = 16.7% (1)
Jordan: (28-22)/22 x 100 = 27.3%
Jordan showed the greatest percentage improvement at 27.3% (1). [Accept working shown for any calculation; final identification of Jordan with correct value earns the last mark.]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which fitness testing provides useful information to a 16-year-old competitive long-distance runner preparing for an important race in six weeks' time.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: For — fitness tests identify the runner's current cardiovascular endurance (Cooper 12-minute run), muscular endurance (press-up test) and flexibility (sit and reach), giving a precise starting point; results compared to normative data reveal specific weaknesses; the six-week timeline means test-retest at the end can measure improvement and inform whether training has been effective; data provides motivation and objective targets. Against — some tests have limitations: the Cooper test gives a valid snapshot but conditions (weather, surface, fatigue) affect reproducibility; normative data tables may not reflect elite competitive standards; tests measure components in isolation and cannot replicate race conditions; testing takes time that could be used for training. Conclusion: fitness testing provides valuable baseline data and monitors progress, but the coach should combine test results with race-specific training data for best effect. Balanced, applied, concluded.

Secure: Identifies benefits and at least one limitation. Running context present. Attempted conclusion.

Developing: Discusses benefits with limited limitations. Some sporting application.

Emerging: Names tests or reasons. Little evaluation or sporting context.

knowledge_checks.q: Which fitness test measures cardiovascular endurance by recording how far someone can run in a fixed time?
What does normative data allow a coach to do with a fitness test result?
options: Compare the result against population averages for the same age and gender
Measure the athlete's exact maximum heart rate
Design a complete training programme automatically

knowledge_checks.q: The _____ test measures leg power by recording how high someone can jump above their standing reach.
The sit and reach test measures _____ at the lower back and hamstrings.
Match each fitness test to the component it measures:

flashcard_questions.q: Which fitness test measures cardiovascular endurance using a 12-minute effort?
flashcard_questions.a: The Cooper 12-minute run test (or swim test).

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Harvard Step Test measure?
flashcard_questions.a: Cardiovascular endurance, using heart rate 1 minute after stepping for 5 minutes.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Illinois agility run test measure?
What does the grip dynamometer measure?
Which two tests measure muscular endurance?
flashcard_questions.a: One-minute sit-up test and one-minute press-up test.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the vertical jump test measure?
What does the sit and reach test measure?
flashcard_questions.a: Flexibility at the lower back and hamstrings.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the 30-metre sprint test measure?

flashcard_questions.a: Pre-established result ranges for different age groups and genders, used to evaluate test scores.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the formula for percentage improvement between two test scores?
flashcard_questions.a: (New score minus original score) divided by original score, multiplied by 100.

flashcard_questions.q: Give two reasons why a coach carries out fitness testing.
flashcard_questions.a: To identify strengths and weaknesses, and to monitor improvement over time.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must the correct normative data table be used when comparing fitness test results?
flashcard_questions.a: Expected results vary significantly between age groups and genders.

glossary_terms.definition: The ability of the heart, lungs and circulatory system to supply oxygen to working muscles over a sustained period.
A fitness test in which the participant runs as far as possible in 12 minutes; distance covered is compared against normative tables.
A variation of the Cooper test in which the participant swims as far as possible in 12 minutes.
A step test using a 30 cm bench; the participant steps up and down for 5 minutes and the heart rate 1 minute after stopping is used to calculate a fitness index.
A timed agility test in which the participant weaves through a set cone course as fast as possible; time is compared against norms.
A handheld device that measures the maximum force produced by the hand and forearm muscles when squeezed.
A flexibility test in which the participant sits with legs straight and reaches as far forward as possible along a measuring board.
Pre-established data sets showing expected ranges of fitness test results for different age groups and genders, used to evaluate an individual's score.
